extracted.intended_audience: environmental lawyers, regulators, courts, and stakeholders participating in notice-and-comment on EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A legal and technical petition challenging EPA's rescission of vehicle GHG regulation and its 'futility'/endangerment analysis, focusing on modeling methodology, statutory interpretation, transparency, and procedural adequacy under notice-and-comment. It critiques modeling choices (timeframes, gases included, baselines), reproducibility, and the sufficiency of agency explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical time-horizon must capture long-term impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency’s choice to analyze only these two points in time [2050 and 2100] is arbitrary, because they significantly undervalue the increasing and long-term adverse harms of climate pollution from U.S. vehicles in two critical ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling must extend beyond 2100 to capture persistent and cumulative impacts of GHGs (which persist centuries/millennia) and to account for increasing proportional contributions of U.S. vehicles over time; EPA’s earlier ozone-related modeling extended impacts to the lifespans of persons born through 2100 and therefore effectively to ~2175—EPA must provide a basis for any truncated period and cannot cherry-pick endpoints outside public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for changing proportional contribution over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EPA’s framework, the proportional contribution of U.S. vehicles to global emissions is anticipated to increase over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should not treat U.S. contributions as static; modeling must reflect how the U.S. vehicle share of global emissions can grow (e.g., from ~4% in 2027 to ~10% in 2100 in EPA's own modeling) and include later years where proportional contributions may be much larger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include persistence and accumulation of GHGs (cumulative impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: GHG emissions accumulate in the atmosphere and continue to affect the physical climate for centuries and even millennia after their release; modeling only through 2100 arbitrarily ignores persistent and cumulative impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models must represent stacking/accumulation of annual emissions and long atmospheric lifetimes of different GHGs (and consequent long-term climate responses), not truncate impacts at arbitrary calendar dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and report all relevant greenhouse gases, not CO2-only
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA arbitrarily excluded vehicular emissions of nitrous oxide (N2O), methane (CH4), and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) from its analysis, even though motor vehicles unquestionably emit such gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Futility or impact analyses must include N2O, CH4, and HFCs (and other relevant GHGs); omission is unsupportable, particularly where EPA has previously modeled them or where they have high GWP (e.g., HFCs from A/C leakage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot excuse exclusion of pollutants by pointing to separate legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA appears to suggest that its futility analysis disregarded vehicle HFC emissions because there is 'separately enacted legislation requiring a phase out of HFCs' under a different section of the Clean Air Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must not treat separate statutory programs (e.g., the AIM Act) as displacing section 202(a) authority; statutory complements do not justify omission of pollutants from a section 202(a) analysis, and prior EPA practice modeling HFCs under vehicle rules shows such exclusion lacks rational justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and reproducibility of modeling and inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA failed to adequately document its data and methodology, rendering its results not reproducible by the public and violating both the legal requirements of CAA section 307(d) and prevailing scientific norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must disclose emissions inputs for all modeled years (not just ~4% of years), modeling files for all models used (OMEGA, MOVES, FaIR, BRICK), model versions, key parameters, and other files necessary to reproduce runs; omission of such materials prevents meaningful public critique and violates notice-and-comment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose model versions, parameters, and run files
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not disclose many of the key parameters that would have enabled Petitioners to reproduce EPA’s model runs (e.g., BRICK model version).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must identify the exact model versions, parameters, and configuration files used for each model run; providing partial model files for some models is insufficient for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on a single scenario or single set of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutability of the results further highlights the arbitrary nature of EPA’s reliance on only one modeling scenario, calculated based on a single set of assumptions, and never subjected to public scrutiny through notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should run and present multiple scenarios (sensitivity analyses) with different baseline years, emissions inputs, and assumptions (e.g., Scenarios A, B, C) and analyze how results change; choosing only one scenario to support a sweeping legal conclusion is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate baseline selection (do not bake-in program benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even assuming the basic framework of EPA’s modeling approach—the Agency would have to show that any such standards would be futile, not only a standard commencing with MY2027 and beyond. EPA's choice of a 2027 baseline bakes in benefits of the GHG program and is inappropriate when assessing whether all standards are futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming futility of a regulatory scheme, the appropriate counterfactual baseline is the absence of the GHG program (or at least multiple baselines); baselines that already assume emissions reductions from prior regulation distort an analysis of whether regulation itself is futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model fleet turnover using established methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are well-established methodologies for calculating the rate of fleet turnover, including the methodologies applied by EPA in its MOVES model; applying those methodologies, we can quantify the emissions attributable to new MY2027 and later vehicles in any given year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must account for fleet turnover dynamics (not flatline emissions after 2055), quantify contributions of new model-year vehicles over time, and justify any simplifications with reference to standard methods; arbitrary flatlining or crude assumptions distort results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not arbitrarily flatline emissions in late years
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenario B also corrects EPA’s arbitrary choice to flatline emissions after 2055.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling should not impose unjustified flatlines or cutoffs in emissions projections; any end-of-horizon assumptions must be explained and supported by evidence or sensitivity testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative scenarios must be fully documented and analytically justified
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Rule posits an 'illustrative' 50% reduction scenario ... only in the preamble text without any technical documentation, yet the Agency’s futility finding relies critically on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting illustrative reductions (e.g., '50% reduction'), EPA must provide emissions inputs, modeling runs, methodological detail, and rationale; an undocumented illustrative factor that materially affects conclusions is arbitrary and unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot manufacture results by scaling model outputs ex post
rubrics_metrics.description: It appears the Agency did not perform global temperature or global sea level rise modeling for the illustrative scenario at all; instead, it merely multiplied the modeled global temperature and sea level rise outputs for the original scenario ... by 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must rerun climate and sea-level models (e.g., BRICK, FaIR) with the alternative emissions inputs rather than simply scaling outputs; complex physical climate processes do not justify linear back-of-the-napkin scaling of modeled outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and defend any de minimis threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Notably, EPA claims that 'courts have consistently viewed impacts of 1% as de minimis' (an erroneous assertion we further critique). EPA’s 1% de minimis threshold is also arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency relies on a quantitative de minimis threshold (e.g., 1%), it must justify that threshold with legal and scientific evidence; arbitrary numeric cutoffs unsupported by precedent or analysis are vulnerable to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider regional and distributional impacts, not only global averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Many American communities will bear far greater impacts than suggested by these global average figures. Global average temperature increases are not distributed evenly across space ... Arctic Alaska warming at three times the global average rate ... local sea level rise along the U.S. coast of the Gulf of Mexico demonstrates that the Gulf is projected to suffer substantially greater local sea level rise impacts than the global average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must evaluate spatial heterogeneity and distributional consequences (regional/local temperature and sea-level impacts, disproportionate effects on vulnerable communities), not rely solely on global average metrics when assessing welfare/harm and legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization of damages must use transparent, accepted methods and disclose assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: To monetize the harms of U.S. vehicle GHG emissions, Petitioners also evaluated the social costs of GHGs (SC-GHG) ... Petitioners calculated SC-GHG assuming the Final Rule’s methodology of projecting emissions, global temperature, and sea level impacts ... we project that EPA’s estimated level of U.S. vehicle GHGs will cause $17.6 trillion in global climate change damages through 2100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting monetized harms (SC-GHG), the agency or commenters must state the SC-GHG method used, discount rates, time horizons, and assumptions; monetized estimates should be transparently derived and sensitivity-tested (e.g., different discount rates, horizons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess ancillary harms of rescinding standards
rubrics_metrics.description: These figures do not account for other sources of harm associated with fewer clean vehicles, such as criteria pollutant damages, lost consumer fuel savings, energy security harms, and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses must consider co-benefits and non-GHG harms/benefits (criteria pollutants, consumer savings, energy security) when evaluating the consequences of rescission or reversal of standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must provide adequate notice and opportunity for public comment on key data and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: This reinforces both the gravity of EPA’s procedural error in not providing the public with notice and opportunity to comment on these key data and methodological assumptions, as well as the substantive arbitrariness of EPA’s determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key data, modeling assumptions, and methodological choices that materially affect regulatory conclusions must be disclosed in the proposal so that stakeholders can comment; hiding or failing to disclose such information violates notice-and-comment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and justify departures from prior agency practice
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s truncated modeling time-period contrasts sharply with how the Agency assesses the harm done by ozone-depleting chemicals ... EPA has not provided any basis for adopting a more truncated time period in this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency uses a different timeframe, metric, or method than in prior analogous rulemakings, it must explain and justify the departure; unexplained inconsistency is evidence of arbitrary decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete and matching model outputs and claimed emissions values
rubrics_metrics.description: While EPA did provide MOVES5.R1 and MOVES5.R2 modeling files upon Petitioners’ request to the EPA Docket Center, the outputs from these provided files do not match EPA’s stated emission values in its futility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must ensure that provided model runs and outputs coincide with numbers reported in the preamble/technical memos; discrepancies must be explained and corrected so that the public can verify results.
